KEY MESSAGE 1... 

Insolation within a slightly more humid air mass today has 
generated surface-based instability values to 1000 - 2000 
J/Kg. Lingering weak troughing overhead and associated cool 
pool aloft has resulted in isolated to scattered thunderstorms 
this afternoon focused mainly in the terrain including the 
southern Greens, western MA, Litchfield Hills, and parts of the
Upper Hudson Valley. Convection will be mainly diurnally driven
but a few showers may last through about Midnight. Very weak 
shear aloft will keep storm slow moving and allow for locally 
heavy downpours to occur; however, severe weather is not
anticipated.

There is increasing confidence for periods of moderate to heavy
to develop tomorrow afternoon lasting into tomorrow night. This
will occur as our parent shortwave currently in the Midwest 
rounds the top of the expansive ridge through the Central CONUS
and amplifies as it tracks into the eastern Great Lakes 
tomorrow. Strong upper level diffluence will allow the sfc low 
that will be in western NY to deepen resulting in a 
strengthening south-southeasterly low-level jet. This will lead
to a strong and deep moisture fetch from the Gulf and western 
Atlantic with PWATs reaching near 2" resulting in periods of 
moderate to heavy rain. Initial scattered showers tomorrow
morning reaching parts of eastern NY and western New England
will transition to more organized areas of moderate to even
heavy rain from west to east by 15 - 18 UTC continuing into the
overnight hours as the impressive moisture fetch ahead of the
low continues to be directed into the Northeast. Mean cloud
layer winds look to be oriented nearly parallel to the low-level
jet through 09-12 UTC Wednesday and with freezing heights 12 -
13kft and tall skinny CAPE soundings, efficient warm rain
processes capable of producing heavy downpours will be at play.
The unidirectional flow also suggests training convection or 
heavy rain repeatedly impacting a given area, raising concerns 
for flash flooding. The overall dynamics with this event are 
quite impressive for July with the NAEFS showing height 
anomalies 3 to 4 standard deviations below normal as the parent
trough closes off into Wednesday with integrated water vapor 
transport 3-4 standard deviations above normal due to the high
V-wind component anomalies and PWATs. Latest probabilistic 
guidance from the HREF shows 40 to 60% chance for 1 inch of rain
falling in 3 hours from early afternoon tomorrow through 
Tuesday night including even 15 to 30% chance for over 2 inches 
in 3 hours. This indicates multiple hours where high rainfall 
rates can reach 1 to 2 inches per hour at times with even 
locally higher amounts possible. The highest probabilities for 
high rainfall rates reside in the eastern Catskills due to 
favorable upslope enhancements. 

While our recent stretch of dry weather has led to high flash
flood guidance (FFG) values including 2-2.5 inches in 1 hour and 2-3
inches in 3 hrs, training convection and heavy rain persisting
over a given area for multiple hours can quickly overcome a dry
ground resulting in flash flooding. In collaboration with WPC
and neighboring WFOs, the heavy rain signal was strong enough
for us to issue a Flash Flood Watch for areas mainly south of
I-90 from 18 UTC Tues to 00 UTC Thurs with WPC upgrading the Day
2 Excessive Rainfall Outlook to a moderate risk (level 3 of 4)
to message potential for numerous instances of flash flooding.
There is a slight risk (level 2 of 4) for excessive rainfall for
most of the other parts of the area.

KEY MESSAGE 2...

Our parent cyclone becomes a vertically stacked closes low by 
Wednesday and slows down as it shifts into eastern NY. The
moisture plume shifts into New England but continues to wrap 
around the low throughout the day on Wednesday supporting
continued periods of steady rain. Not only will steady rain
bands continue within the deformation zone on the north/west of
the low but there are signals of a TROWAL developing with weak 
instability aloft supporting periods of moderate to heavy rain.
Given the heavy rain from Tuesday into Tuesday night, soils 
will likely be saturated and therefore more vulnerable to 
flooding. At this point, we will likely transition more to areal
flooding versus flash flooding as many will be raining for 
nearly 24 hours at that point but nonetheless, additional 
flooding concerns continue into Wednesday and our Flood Watch
therefore continues through 8PM Wednesday. Despite the long 
duration of this rain event, the latest MMEFS and Northeast 
River Forecast Center still indicate no flooding concerns. Wrap 
around rain continue into Wednesday night and even Thursday as
the low will be very slow to exit into New England. Otherwise,
temperatures Wednesday and Thursday will remain below normal
likely struggling to rise out of the 60s to low 70s given ample
cloud coverage and rain.
